source_text: Free chlorine (FC) is the portion of chlorine in pool water that has not yet reacted with contaminants.
It exists primarily as hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and hypochlorite ion (OCl−).
HOCl is the active sanitizing form and is 40–80× more effective than OCl−.
The ratio of HOCl to OCl− is determined by pH — lower pH means more HOCl.
Free chlorine must be maintained above the minimum level dictated by the cyanuric acid concentration.
Combined chlorine (CC) is the difference between total chlorine and free chlorine.
It consists primarily of chloramines — compounds formed when chlorine reacts with ammonia, urea, and other nitrogen compounds from bathers.
Chloramines are responsible for the "pool smell," eye irritation, and respiratory irritation often mistakenly blamed on too much chlorine.
When CC exceeds 0.5 ppm, breakpoint chlorination (shock treatment) is required.
Total chlorine (TC) equals free chlorine plus combined chlorine.
Most DPD-based test kits measure total chlorine directly, while free chlorine requires a separate reagent.
Combined chlorine is calculated as TC minus FC.
Total chlorine by itself tells you little about water safety — what matters is the free chlorine level and how much has become combined.
Bromine is an alternative to chlorine as a pool and spa sanitizer.
It is more stable than chlorine at high temperatures and high pH, making it popular for hot tubs.
Unlike chlorine, bromine can be regenerated by adding an oxidizer — the bromamines formed are still effective sanitizers.
Bromine cannot be stabilized with cyanuric acid, making it unsuitable for outdoor pools exposed to direct sunlight.
Cyanuric acid (CYA) — also called stabilizer or conditioner — binds to free chlorine to protect it from UV photolysis.
Without CYA, outdoor pool chlorine can degrade to near-zero within 30–60 minutes in direct sunlight.
However, CYA also reduces chlorine's activity.
As CYA increases, the minimum effective free chlorine level must increase proportionally.
CYA above 80–100 ppm causes chlorine lock, where chlorine is present but largely ineffective.
CYA cannot be reduced chemically — only dilution by partial drain and refill removes it.
Calcium hardness (CH) is the measure of dissolved calcium ions in pool water.
It is one of the five variables in the Langelier Saturation Index.
Water with low calcium is aggressive — it will dissolve calcium from plaster, grout, and equipment.
Water with high calcium is scale-forming — calcium carbonate precipitates on surfaces and inside equipment.
The ideal range depends on pool surface type: plaster pools need higher calcium (200–400 ppm) than vinyl or fiberglass pools (150–250 ppm).
Calcium hardness can only be lowered through partial drain and refill.
Pool salt is pure sodium chloride (NaCl) added to pool water for use with a salt chlorinator (also called a saltwater generator or SWCG).
The system electrolytically converts dissolved salt into hypochlorous acid — the same active disinfectant as manually added chlorine.
Salt level must stay within the system's specified range (typically 2,700–3,400 ppm) for the cell to operate efficiently.
Salt does not evaporate; the level only drops through dilution from rain or water replacement.
Human sweat is saltier than a properly maintained salt pool.
Total dissolved solids (TDS) is the sum of all inorganic and organic substances dissolved in pool water — minerals, chemicals, byproducts of sanitization, bather waste, and more.
TDS increases over time as chemicals are added and water evaporates.
The only remedy is partial or full water replacement.
In hot tubs, TDS above 1,500 ppm over the baseline is a standard trigger for water change.
Phosphates are compounds containing phosphorus (PO4³⁻) that enter pool water from bather waste, lawn fertilizer runoff, fill water, and certain pool chemicals.
Phosphates are a primary nutrient for algae.
While low phosphate levels alone do not cause algae (chlorine control is paramount), very high phosphate levels (above 500–1,000 ppb) can reduce chlorine effectiveness and increase algae risk.
Phosphate removers are available but their necessity is debated — good chlorine management prevents algae regardless of phosphate level.
At elevated levels (above 0.3 ppm), copper causes green staining of pool surfaces and hair.
This is often confused with algae but is actually copper oxidation.
Corrosive water (low LSI) accelerates copper leaching from equipment.
Iron in pool water typically comes from well water used to fill the pool or from corroded steel equipment.
When chlorine is added, dissolved ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) is oxidized to ferric iron (Fe³⁺), which is insoluble and precipitates as rust-brown staining on pool walls, floors, and equipment.
Treatment involves metal sequestrants to keep iron in solution, then gradual removal through filtration.
Prevention focuses on fill water quality and maintaining a slightly positive LSI to prevent equipment corrosion.
Like iron, it stains pool surfaces when oxidized — manganese stains are typically black or dark brown/purple rather than the rust-red of iron.
Metal sequestrants hold manganese in solution to prevent precipitation.
Testing with a metal test kit distinguishes manganese from other staining causes.
Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is used as an oxidizer in biguanide (polyhexamethylene biguanide, or PHMB) pool systems, which use hydrogen peroxide rather than chlorine for sanitization.

In chlorine pools, hydrogen peroxide can be used to rapidly reduce excess chlorine in emergencies, but the two chemicals react violently if mixed in concentrated form — always add to pool water separately, never mix directly.
Hydrogen peroxide-based systems require dedicated equipment and are incompatible with chlorine.
Ozone (O₃) is a powerful oxidizing agent generated on-site by UV lamps or corona discharge generators and injected into pool return water.
Because ozone dissipates quickly (it does not accumulate in pool water), it must always be used alongside a residual sanitizer — typically free chlorine at reduced levels.
Ozone does not replace chlorine; it reduces the chlorine demand and helps maintain water clarity and quality with less total chemical use.
Biguanide (sold as Baquacil, SoftSwim, and similar brands) is a chlorine-free pool sanitization system using polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) as the sanitizer and hydrogen peroxide as the oxidizer.
It does not interact with CYA, pH resistance is broader, and it does not bleach surfaces or swimwear.
However, biguanide is incompatible with chlorine — switching between systems requires a complete water change.
It is more expensive than chlorine and some users experience algae resistance issues.
pH is the scale from 0 to 14 measuring how acidic or alkaline pool water is.
A pH of 7.0 is neutral; below 7.0 is acidic; above 7.0 is alkaline.

pH is affected by every chemical addition and by CO₂ off-gassing.
Oxidation-Reduction Potential (ORP) measures the water's ability to oxidize or sanitize — expressed in millivolts (mV).
A higher ORP indicates greater sanitizing capacity.
Unlike ppm-based chlorine testing, ORP directly measures chlorine's effectiveness considering both concentration and pH.
ORP sensors are used in automated chemical control systems to maintain consistent sanitizing capacity regardless of bather load variations.
Higher temperatures accelerate chlorine demand (halving with every 10°C/18°F drop), shift pH upward, increase scaling tendency (higher LSI), and increase CO₂ off-gassing.
Higher temperatures accelerate chlorine demand (halving with every 10°C/18°F drop), shift pH upward, increase scaling tendency (higher LSI), and increase CO₂ off-gassing.
For hot tubs, temperature is also a primary safety parameter — temperatures above 104°F can cause hyperthermia.
For the LSI calculation, water temperature is a required input since calcium carbonate solubility decreases with rising temperature.
Total alkalinity (TA) measures the concentration of alkaline compounds — primarily bicarbonates, carbonates, and hydroxides — dissolved in pool water.
It acts as a pH buffer, resisting pH swings caused by additions of acid, base, or CO₂.
Low TA causes pH to swing wildly with minor chemical additions (pH bounce).
High TA makes pH very difficult to lower and increases scaling tendency.
Total alkalinity must be adjusted before pH — it determines how much chemical is needed for a given pH change.
The Langelier Saturation Index (LSI) is a mathematical model that combines pH, temperature, calcium hardness, total alkalinity, and TDS into a single balance score.
A score of 0 means water is perfectly balanced for calcium carbonate.
Negative values (below −0.3) indicate corrosive water.
The LSI is the final quality check in the water balancing process — if all individual parameters are in range but the LSI is out of range, the combination still needs adjustment.
The US gallon (approximately 3.785 liters) is the standard unit for measuring pool volume in North America.
All chemical dose calculations for pools require an accurate volume in gallons.
Volume is calculated using length × width × average depth × 7.48 (gallons per cubic foot) for rectangular pools, with shape correction factors for other pool shapes.
A 10% error in pool volume produces a 10% error in every chemical dose calculated.
A 10% error in pool volume produces a 10% error in every chemical dose calculated.
The liter is the SI unit of volume used in metric countries for pool measurements.
While calculators on this site use US gallons as the primary unit, all conversions to and from liters are supported.
Chemical doses calculated in metric units (grams per liter, or mg/L for ppm equivalents) are consistent with the same chemistry but expressed in metric terms.
Parts per million (ppm) is the standard unit of concentration for pool chemistry parameters including free chlorine, alkalinity, calcium hardness, cyanuric acid, and TDS.
1 ppm equals 1 milligram per liter (mg/L) in aqueous solution.
Most pool test kits and digital testers report results in ppm.
The relationship between ppm and actual chemical dose is direct: 1 ppm in a 10,000-gallon pool corresponds to 8.34 mg of the substance dissolved in the water.
Flow rate is measured in gallons per minute (GPM) and represents how much water the pump circulates through the filtration system.
Variable speed pumps can be programmed to run at different flow rates at different times of day, reducing energy consumption while maintaining adequate filtration.
Turnover time is the number of hours required for the pump to move the full pool volume through the filtration system.
PHTA recommends a maximum turnover time of 8 hours for residential pools (one complete turnover in 8 hours or less).
The pool pump is the heart of the pool circulation system.
It draws water from skimmers and main drains, forces it through the filter, heater, and chemical feeders, then returns it through jets.
Single-speed pumps run at one fixed RPM; variable-speed pumps (VSP) can be programmed to run at different speeds, reducing energy consumption by up to 80% compared to single-speed models.
Sand filters use a bed of specially graded silica sand (#20 grade) to capture suspended particles.
When the filter pressure increases 8–10 psi above the clean baseline, the filter needs backwashing — reversing the flow to flush trapped material to waste.
Sand should be replaced every 5–7 years.
Cartridge filters use pleated polyester fabric cartridges to filter pool water.

They provide finer filtration than sand (10–15 microns) without requiring backwashing — only periodic cartridge removal, rinsing with a hose, and occasional overnight soaking in cartridge cleaning solution.
Cartridges should be replaced every 12–18 months.
Diatomaceous earth (DE) filters use a fine powder made from fossilized diatoms (microscopic algae) as the filter media.
Maintenance involves backwashing (which removes the used DE) followed by adding fresh DE through the skimmer.
DE must be handled carefully as fine particles can be an inhalation hazard.
Internal grids require annual cleaning and periodic inspection.
They use a weir (floating flap) to create a surface current that draws floating leaves, insects, sunscreen, and debris into a basket before the debris sinks to the pool floor.
The skimmer basket should be checked and emptied regularly — a clogged basket restricts pump flow.
Never add granular shock directly to the skimmer; it can damage equipment.
Skimmers also contain a suction port used during pool vacuuming.
Solar systems have no operating cost but depend on sun availability and add time to the system.
All heater types affect pool chemistry: higher water temperatures increase chlorine demand, pH rise, and LSI scaling tendency.
Heater bypasses allow chemistry adjustment at lower temperatures to extend equipment life.

A salt chlorinator (also called a saltwater generator or SWCG) uses electrolysis to convert sodium chloride dissolved in pool water into hypochlorous acid — the same active disinfectant as manually added chlorine.
The cell consists of titanium plates coated with a precious metal catalyst.
The pool still uses chlorine — it is simply generated on-site from salt rather than added directly.
Salt cells have a lifespan of 3–7 years depending on water chemistry and maintenance.
The cell requires specific salt concentration (usually 2,700–3,400 ppm) and proper water chemistry to avoid premature calcium scaling of the plates.
They automate baseline chlorine maintenance between manual chemical additions.
Because trichlor contains CYA (58% by weight), regular use of tablet feeders gradually accumulates CYA in the water.
Feeders should be set to maintain 1–3 ppm FC and supplemented with liquid chlorine or shock as needed.
Chemical feeders include erosion feeders (for solid products), peristaltic pump systems (for liquid chemicals), and ORP/pH automated controllers.
Automated chemical feed systems monitor ORP and pH in real time and inject the appropriate chemicals to maintain setpoints.
They reduce manual chemical handling and maintain more consistent water chemistry than periodic manual addition.

Pool covers serve multiple functions: safety (hard covers and nets prevent accidental entry), heat retention (solar and thermal covers reduce heat loss and heating costs), water conservation (reduce evaporation by up to 95%), chemical conservation (reduce UV degradation of chlorine and reduce debris-driven chemical demand), and debris exclusion (keep leaves and insects out).
Safety covers are required by law in many jurisdictions for unattended residential pools.

Shock treatment (superchlorination) involves raising free chlorine to a high level — typically 10 ppm for maintenance, 10× the combined chlorine level for breakpoint chlorination, or 30 ppm for algae recovery — to eliminate combined chlorine, algae, bacteria, and other contaminants.

Use calcium hypochlorite (65%) or liquid chlorine (sodium hypochlorite) for chlorine shocking.
Non-chlorine shock (potassium monopersulfate) oxidizes contaminants without adding chlorine — useful when swimming must resume quickly.
Always shock after dark to prevent UV degradation of the added chlorine.
Breakpoint chlorination is the process of adding enough chlorine to destroy all combined chlorine (chloramines) in pool water.
The breakpoint dose is approximately 10 times the current combined chlorine level.
Below this threshold, adding chlorine merely adds to combined chlorine; above it, all combined chlorine is oxidized and destroyed.
The term "breakpoint" describes the inflection point on the chlorine demand curve where adding more chlorine actually increases free chlorine rather than increasing combined chlorine.
Combined chlorine above 0.5 ppm is the trigger for breakpoint chlorination.
Backwashing is the process of reversing water flow through a sand or DE filter to dislodge and flush accumulated debris.
It is initiated when the filter pressure gauge reads 8–10 psi above the clean baseline.

The multiport valve is turned to "Backwash," the pump is run until water runs clear (typically 2–5 minutes), then switched to "Rinse" for 30–60 seconds to reseat the sand before returning to "Filter." Backwashing removes water from the pool — factor this into water level management.
DE filters require adding fresh DE powder after backwashing to recharged the filter grids.

Winterization (pool closing) involves a specific sequence of steps to protect pool equipment and surfaces from freeze damage during cold weather: balancing water chemistry, adding winter chemicals (algaecide, scale inhibitor), draining water below skimmers and jets, blowing out plumbing lines, plugging returns, removing and storing equipment, and covering the pool.
Hot tub winterization involves either proper insulation and continuous low-level heating, or full draining.

Pool opening (spring start-up) is the systematic process of bringing a winterized pool back into service: removing the cover and cleaning it, removing winter plugs and reinstalling equipment, reconnecting the pump and filter, filling to proper water level, starting the pump and checking for leaks, then testing and balancing all water chemistry parameters before the first swim.
Pool opening chemistry typically requires more adjustment than weekly maintenance because water chemistry changes significantly during winter shutdown.
A complete water balance is the final step before opening for swimming.
Water replacement (partial or full drain and refill) is the only way to reduce CYA, calcium hardness, TDS, and salt when they exceed maximum levels.
A partial drain replaces a percentage of the water — a 50% drain reduces all dissolved compounds by 50%.
Hot tubs require complete water changes every 3–4 months due to high bather-to-water ratios that accelerate TDS and combined chlorine accumulation.
Pool partial drains are typically 25–50% and are triggered by CYA above 80 ppm, calcium above 500 ppm, or TDS above 3,000 ppm.

Filtration is the continuous process of circulating pool water through a filter to remove suspended particles — algae, dust, debris, dead skin cells, and other particulate matter.
Effective filtration requires adequate pump flow rate, properly sized filter, regular cleaning, and sufficient daily pump run time.
Filtration does not replace chemical sanitization but works synergistically — the filter removes the physical matter that would otherwise increase chemical demand.
Water testing is the foundation of pool maintenance.
Accurate, regular testing of free chlorine, combined chlorine, pH, alkalinity, calcium hardness, and CYA enables correct chemical dosing.
Test methods include: test strips (fast but less precise), DPD liquid test kits (more accurate, color-based), digital photometric testers (highest accuracy), and professional testing by a pool store.
Testing frequency varies by parameter: FC and pH should be tested twice weekly; alkalinity and calcium monthly.
Test before every soak in a hot tub.
Sanitizing is the ongoing process of maintaining sufficient disinfectant (free chlorine, bromine, or alternative) to kill bacteria, viruses, and other pathogens in pool water.

Effective sanitization requires maintaining free chlorine above the minimum level for the current CYA concentration, ensuring pH is in the 7.2–7.6 range where HOCl is maximally effective, and providing adequate turnover for the disinfectant to contact all parts of the pool.
Sanitizing is distinct from oxidizing — both are needed for safe, clear pool water.
Oxidation is the chemical reaction that destroys organic matter, combined chlorine (chloramines), swimmer waste, and other contaminants in pool water.
While free chlorine both sanitizes (kills pathogens) and oxidizes (destroys organic matter), pools with high bather loads may have more oxidation demand than chlorine sanitization demand.
Non-chlorine oxidizers (potassium monopersulfate, hydrogen peroxide) can handle the oxidation load while preserving free chlorine for sanitization.
Regular oxidation keeps combined chlorine low, prevents chlorine odor, and maintains water clarity.
Water balancing is the comprehensive process of adjusting pH, total alkalinity, calcium hardness, CYA, and free chlorine to achieve a stable, safe, and non-damaging water chemistry.
The correct order matters: adjust alkalinity first (it determines how much acid/base is needed for pH), then pH, then calcium hardness, then CYA, then chlorine.
The final check is the LSI — if all individual parameters are in range, the LSI confirms the combination is balanced.
Properly balanced water protects equipment, surfaces, and swimmers.

The Pool Maintenance Checklist is a free printable resource that guides residential pool owners through weekly pool care: testing water chemistry, adding chemicals, cleaning skimmer baskets, brushing walls, checking filter pressure, and verifying equipment operation.
Following a consistent checklist prevents the buildup of problems that lead to expensive treatments.
The Hot Tub Maintenance Log tracks daily and weekly spa chemistry readings, chemical doses, filter cleaning, and water change dates.
It is especially useful for vacation rental operators who must demonstrate chemical compliance and for multi-property managers tracking chemical costs.
The Vacation Rental Pool Turnover Checklist provides a structured protocol for testing, adjusting, and documenting pool chemistry at the start of each guest stay.
It covers safety equipment inspection, water chemistry testing, chemical additions, filter check, and safety communication to incoming guests.
Used consistently, it reduces liability exposure and ensures every guest has safe pool access.

The Water Test Log provides a structured format for recording all pool or hot tub chemistry test results over time: free chlorine, pH, alkalinity, calcium hardness, CYA, salt, and any notes on chemical additions or pool events.
Tracking readings over time reveals chemistry trends, helps diagnose recurring problems, and supports informed decisions about when water replacement is needed.

The Pool Opening Checklist guides pool owners through the spring startup process: removing the cover, reinstalling equipment, filling to proper level, starting the pump, and completing a full water balance before the first swim.
It provides space for recording test results and chemical additions during the opening process.

The Pool Closing Checklist provides a structured process for winterizing a pool: balancing chemistry, adding winter chemicals, lowering water level, blowing out plumbing, installing freeze plugs, removing equipment, and covering the pool.
Proper winterization prevents expensive freeze damage.

The Emergency Recovery Reference provides concise protocols for the most urgent pool chemistry situations: green pool recovery, zero chlorine restoration, chemical overdose response, and equipment failure response.

Cloudy water can result from low free chlorine (allowing algae or bacteria to proliferate), pH or alkalinity out of range (causing precipitation or flocculation), calcium carbonate precipitation (scaling, especially after shock), high TDS, poor filtration (pump run time too low, dirty filter, inadequate turnover), or dissolved metals.
Start by testing all parameters, correcting chemistry, and running the filter continuously until clarity returns.
Green pool water is almost always caused by an algae bloom — typically green algae — resulting from insufficient free chlorine.
Contributing factors include CYA too high (reducing chlorine effectiveness), missed shock treatments, heavy rain (diluting chlorine), extended periods without service, or pump failure.
Treatment involves lowering pH to 7.2 to maximize chlorine activity, brushing all surfaces, shocking to 30 ppm FC, and running the filter 24 hours.

The water may turn grey as algae dies, then clear over 24–72 hours as the dead algae is filtered out.
Foam on pool or hot tub water is caused by surfactants — substances that lower water surface tension.

Mild foaming can be treated with an anti-foam agent as a temporary fix, but the underlying cause must be addressed: rinsing swimwear without soap, showering before entering, reducing algaecide dose, or changing the water if TDS is very high.
Scaling is the precipitation of calcium carbonate and other minerals onto pool surfaces, tile lines, plumbing, and equipment.
It is caused by over-saturated water (positive LSI), which occurs when pH, calcium hardness, alkalinity, or temperature is too high.
Treatment requires lowering the LSI by adjusting pH, alkalinity, and calcium hardness.
Existing scale can be removed with acid washing or mechanical removal, but this should be done by a professional to avoid surface damage.
Corrosion occurs when pool water is under-saturated with calcium carbonate (negative LSI), causing it to aggressively dissolve calcium from plaster, grout, and metal surfaces.
Visible signs include pitting of plaster surfaces, etching of tile grout, staining from dissolved metals (green from copper, rust from iron), and corrosion of metal fittings.
Contributing factors include low pH, low alkalinity, low calcium hardness, and high water temperature.
Treatment involves raising the LSI by adjusting the relevant parameters.
Ongoing corrosion from a heater indicates the LSI needs attention immediately.
Algae are plant-like microorganisms that grow in pool water when free chlorine drops below effective levels.
Green algae is the most common and easiest to treat.
Black algae develops deep root structures that penetrate pool surfaces, making it the most difficult to eradicate.
Algae growth is fueled by nutrients (especially phosphates), warm water, sunlight, and insufficient chlorine.
Prevention requires maintaining adequate free chlorine relative to CYA level at all times.
The "strong chlorine smell" associated with pools is not caused by too much free chlorine — it is caused by combined chlorine (chloramines).

When free chlorine reacts with nitrogen compounds from bathers (urea, ammonia, amino acids), it forms chloramines that have a strong, distinctive odor and are irritating to eyes and respiratory tract.
Paradoxically, the solution is to add MORE chlorine (breakpoint chlorination) to destroy the chloramines, not less.
A well-maintained pool with low combined chlorine should have little to no chlorine smell.
Eye irritation from pool water is most commonly caused by chloramines (combined chlorine) or pH outside the 7.2–7.8 range.
Human tears have a pH of approximately 7.4 — water at the same pH is least irritating to eyes.
At lower pH, the water is acidic and irritating; at higher pH, chlorine effectiveness drops and chloramines accumulate.
The fix for chloramine-induced eye irritation is breakpoint chlorination.
The fix for pH-related eye irritation is adjusting pH to 7.2–7.6.

Skin irritation after pool or hot tub use can result from pH too far outside the neutral range (below 7.0 or above 8.0), high combined chlorine (chloramines), very high free chlorine (above 5 ppm), high bromine (above 10 ppm), or individual sensitivity to pool chemicals.

Persistent skin irritation despite normal chemistry may indicate individual chemical sensitivity.
Low free chlorine is the single most common and dangerous pool chemistry problem.
When FC drops below the minimum for the current CYA level, the pool loses its primary protection against pathogens and algae.
Causes include: heavy bather loads, hot sunny weather (UV degradation), CYA too high (reducing chlorine activity), insufficient dosing frequency, or empty chlorinator.
The remedy is immediate addition of chlorine to restore FC to the target range.
If CYA is above 80 ppm, a partial drain may be needed before chlorine can be maintained effectively.
High free chlorine (above 5 ppm) causes bleaching of swimwear, eye and skin irritation, and respiratory irritation in enclosed spaces.
It occurs after an accidental over-dose, feeder malfunction, or over-shocking.
The pool should be closed to swimmers until FC drops below 5 ppm (3 ppm for hot tubs).
The pool should be closed to swimmers until FC drops below 5 ppm (3 ppm for hot tubs).
Natural dissipation by sunlight and time is the safest remedy.
Sodium thiosulfate can neutralize chlorine in emergencies but should be used sparingly — reducing FC too quickly can cause a rebound.
Running the pump without cover during daylight hours accelerates UV degradation of excess chlorine.
Low pH (below 7.2) makes pool water corrosive and irritating.
Effects include: etching of plaster and grout surfaces, staining from dissolved metals, corrosion of metal equipment and fittings, eye and skin irritation, and degradation of seals and gaskets.
Low pH is commonly caused by adding too much acid, CO₂ from bather respiration, heavy rain (which is naturally acidic), and naturally acidic fill water.
Treatment involves adding soda ash (sodium carbonate) to raise pH, after first verifying alkalinity is in range.
High pH (above 7.8) significantly reduces free chlorine effectiveness — at pH 8.0, only 22% of FC is in the active HOCl form (compared to 67% at pH 7.2).

High pH also promotes scaling (high positive LSI), causes eye irritation through a different mechanism than low pH, and can cause white cloudiness from calcium carbonate precipitation.
High pH commonly results from adding too much soda ash, sodium bicarbonate increasing pH as a side effect, CO₂ off-gassing from aeration (waterfalls, jets), and some source water.
Treatment involves adding muriatic acid (hydrochloric acid) or dry acid (sodium bisulfate).
Standard pool chemistry applies to all pool types, with adjustments for surface material, volume, and usage pattern.
Most residential pools hold 10,000–30,000 gallons and require weekly chemical maintenance.
A saltwater pool is a chlorine pool that generates its own chlorine using a salt chlorinator (SWCG).
The pool still contains and uses chlorine — the salt content (typically 3,000–3,200 ppm) is far lower than ocean water (35,000 ppm) and is often described as similar to natural tears.
The pool still contains and uses chlorine — the salt content (typically 3,000–3,200 ppm) is far lower than ocean water (35,000 ppm) and is often described as similar to natural tears.
Salt pools still require the same chemistry balancing (pH, alkalinity, calcium, CYA) as traditionally chlorinated pools.
Key differences include higher CYA requirements (60–80 ppm), consistent monitoring of the salt cell, and the risk of calcium scaling on the cell at low LSI.
Indoor pools present unique challenges: without UV light, chlorine is not degraded and CYA is not needed (and is actually counterproductive in indoor settings).
Ventilation is critical — pool rooms must exchange air continuously to remove chloramine vapors and prevent moisture damage to the structure.
pH tends to rise in indoor pools due to CO₂ off-gassing into enclosed air.
Cyanuric acid should not be used in indoor pools.
Outdoor pools are exposed to UV light that rapidly degrades free chlorine.
Cyanuric acid (CYA) is essential for stabilizing chlorine in outdoor pools — without it, sunlight can destroy the chlorine within 30–60 minutes.
Summer requires more frequent chlorine dosing due to both UV degradation and higher bather loads.
A hot tub (spa) is a small, heated body of water — typically 75–500 gallons — used for soaking, relaxation, and hydrotherapy.

The chemistry challenges are significant: high water temperature accelerates chemical reactions and chlorine demand; small volume means even one bather produces a significant bather load relative to total water; the high bather-to-water ratio causes rapid chemistry changes.
Hot tub water should be tested before every soak session and changed every 3–4 months under typical use.
Typically 12–20 feet long and holding 1,000–2,000 gallons, swim spas have a jet system that creates a current for swimming in place.

Commercial pools (public pools, hotel pools, club pools) are subject to state and local health department regulations that typically require stricter chemistry standards than residential pools — often a maximum 6-hour or even 4-hour turnover rate, specific free chlorine and pH ranges, mandatory ORP monitoring, and documented chemical logs.
Vinyl liner pools have a flexible PVC liner as the pool surface.
They require lower calcium hardness (150–250 ppm) than plaster pools because the liner itself does not dissolve calcium.
Low calcium is less of a concern for vinyl pools from a surface damage perspective, but very aggressive water can still attack metal parts and fittings.
Vinyl liners can be bleached by direct contact with undissolved granular chemicals — always pre-dissolve shock and calcium chloride before adding.
Liners typically last 8–15 years before replacement.
Fiberglass pools have a smooth, non-porous fiberglass surface that is inherently resistant to algae (fewer attachment points) and requires less maintenance than plaster pools.
Calcium hardness targets are lower (150–250 ppm) than plaster pools.
Very low calcium in aggressive water can leach the gelcoat surface over time.
The smooth surface also means less chemical demand overall.
Fiberglass pools cannot be refinished in the same way as plaster, so maintaining proper water chemistry to protect the surface is especially important.
Concrete pools (gunite or shotcrete) have a plaster, aggregate (pebble), or tile surface applied over a concrete shell.
These surfaces are porous and contain calcium — aggressive water (low LSI) actively dissolves calcium from the surface, causing etching, pitting, and roughness.
Calcium hardness must be maintained at 200–400 ppm for plaster pools to prevent surface damage.
Concrete pools are durable and highly customizable but require more careful chemistry management than vinyl or fiberglass pools.
Liquid chlorine is sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) solution, typically sold at 10–12.5% available chlorine for pool use (compared to 5–8.25% for household bleach).
It is the most widely used chlorine product for pool maintenance: fast-dissolving, no residue, does not raise calcium or CYA, and relatively inexpensive.
Degradation: liquid chlorine loses approximately 20–30% potency within 60 days at room temperature and significantly faster in heat.

Calcium hypochlorite (cal-hypo) is a dry granular or tablet chlorine compound available at 65% and 73% available chlorine — the most concentrated of common pool shock products.
It raises free chlorine rapidly and is the preferred product for breakpoint chlorination and algae recovery.
Unlike trichlor and dichlor, it does not add CYA.
However, it does add calcium — relevant in pools with already high calcium hardness.
Must be pre-dissolved in water before adding to the pool; direct application can bleach liners and damage surfaces.
Sodium dichloro-s-triazinetrione (dichlor) is a stabilized granular chlorine compound containing approximately 56–62% available chlorine and 57% CYA by weight.
It dissolves quickly and is convenient for pool shocking, but each pound added raises CYA by approximately 6–7 ppm per 10,000 gallons.

Trichloro-s-triazinetrione (trichlor) tablets contain approximately 90% available chlorine and 58% CYA by weight.
They dissolve slowly and are used in automatic chlorinators, floaters, and skimmer baskets for consistent baseline chlorination.
Very acidic (pH ~2.9) — repeated use will lower pool pH and alkalinity over time.
CYA accumulation from trichlor is the most common cause of high CYA in residential pools.
Should not be mixed with calcium hypochlorite — fire and explosion risk.
Muriatic acid (hydrochloric acid, HCl) at 31.45% concentration is the standard product for lowering pH and total alkalinity in pools.
It reacts quickly and is highly effective but requires careful handling — it is strongly corrosive and produces acidic vapors.
Always add acid to water (not water to acid), pre-dilute in a bucket of pool water, and add near return jets with pump running.
Dry acid (sodium bisulfate) is a safer-handling alternative that produces the same chemistry result.
Store in original container away from chlorine products.
Soda ash (sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃) is the standard product for raising pH in pool water.
Unlike sodium bicarbonate, soda ash primarily raises pH with a modest effect on alkalinity.
Pre-dissolve in a bucket of water before adding to prevent white cloudiness in the pool.

Pool salt is 99.8%+ pure sodium chloride (NaCl) sold specifically for use in saltwater pool systems.
It must be free of additives (no anti-caking agents, iodide, or ferrocyanide) that can stain pools and damage salt cells.
Sold in 40-lb bags; a typical 20,000-gallon pool requires 350–400 lbs to reach the target 3,200 ppm from zero.
Salt does not evaporate and only needs replacement after significant water loss.
The CDC provides guidelines on healthy swimming, recreational water illness prevention, disinfection standards for public pools and water parks, and outbreak reporting.
Their Model Aquatic Health Code (MAHC) provides science-based guidance used as the basis for many state pool health codes.
The EPA regulates the registration, labeling, and use of pesticides and disinfectants in the United States under FIFRA (Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act).
Pool disinfectants — including chlorine products, bromine products, and algaecides — are regulated as pesticides by the EPA.
The Pool & Hot Tub Alliance (formerly APSP) is the primary trade association for pool and spa manufacturers, builders, service technicians, and retailers.
PHTA publishes the Pool & Spa Operator Handbook (the industry standard reference for pool chemistry) and the ANSI standards for pool design, construction, and safety.
PHTA certifications (CPO, ATP) are the recognized professional credentials in the pool industry.
NSF certification marks on pool products indicate independent verification of performance and safety claims.

Minutes are used in pool chemistry for: turnover rate calculations (Volume in gallons / GPM = turnover time in minutes), wait times after chemical additions, and filtration cycle timing.
Hours are the standard unit for expressing pool turnover time, pump daily run time, and wait times for chemical balancing.

Days are used for maintenance scheduling (test twice per week, shock weekly), CYA dissolution time (24–48 days), water change intervals for hot tubs (every 90 days), and chemical activity timelines.
Weeks are the standard interval for pool maintenance activities: weekly water testing, weekly shock treatment (optional), weekly brushing and vacuuming, and weekly filter checks.
Monthly intervals are used for: calcium hardness and CYA testing (monthly), hot tub water changes (every 3–4 months), filter inspection, and salt level verification.
